utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. We are the 17th of August, 2006, today. The hearing has resumed after the summer recess. I would like to greet the representatives from the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, and the accused who are present in the courtroom. As you know, we ruled on a number of points before the 14th of July, so I hope that all the attorneys have been advised of these decisions. There are two decisions which will be taken very shortly. One pertains to a motion filed by the Prosecution pursuant to 94(B), and motions relating to Rule 92 bis. In addition, a decision will shortly be rendered pertaining to Mr. Ibrisimovic's motion relating to documents that have been presented by the Prosecution that were not on the Prosecution's 75 ter list. We will undoubtedly rule on the matter next week. Also, a decision needs to be taken as regards a number of documents pertaining to the witness Manolic. So all in all, we are not running behind time and all the remaining decisions will be taken at the beginning of next week, which means that this trial should unfold in the best conditions possible. We have a witness today. Mr. Mundis, how much time do you expect to be leading this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. My colleague Tonia Gillett will be taking the witness this morning, so perhaps she can answer that question for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I anticipate that the witness should take about two hours for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much. Defence counsel will have up until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- will have up until a quarter to 2.00. I hope on the Defence side that you have decided who will start cross-examining the witness. If you have not decided, as you know, your time will be divided between all six of you. This will include the time for additional questions or re-examination. We shall now ask the usher to go and fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Could you give us your name, please; your surname and Christian name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ibrahim Saric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give me your date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 18th of June, 1946, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a graduate electrical engineer, and I deal in communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me what positions you held in 1992 and 1993, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, at the beginning of the war I worked in the old post office, up to October 1992 or, rather, September. After that, I joined the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified about those events that unfolded in your country in 1992, 1993 before this Tribunal or before any other domestic court, or is it the first time you testify before a court of justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a witness at Mr. -- The Mr. Dzidic et al. trial in Sarajevo, nowhere else. This is the first time I'm testifying before the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like you to read out the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have just told us that you have already testified before a court of justice, you know how the proceedings unfold, but this Trial Chamber is a bit specific. To begin with, you'll have to answer those questions that will be put to you by the Prosecution that are seated to your right. The Prosecution has told us that overall they would need two hours. After the examination-in-chief, the Defence counsel, seated to your left, will put questions to you in what is termed the cross-examination. The four Judges, the Bench which is before you, will also intervene and put questions to you directly sometimes. If you feel uneasy at any point in time, please let us know. I would like to remind you that you have just taken the solemn declaration and therefore you have said that you would speak nothing but the truth. The penalty you could incur, of course, is a penalty for perjury or false testimony. This testimony should end at a quarter to 2.00. We will have two breaks, 20-minute breaks, in the course of the morning, and we need to have these breaks for technical reasons. I shall now give the floor to the representative of the Office of the Prosecution who will start examining you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Saric. Mr. Saric, before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina started, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I lived in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Who were you living with?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was living with my wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: In answer to the Judge's question just a moment ago, you mentioned that you joined the 4th Corps of the Bosnian army. That's right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What was your function within the 4th Corps of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was in charge of the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Where were you based to do your job?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: At the time I joined, the base was in the Vranica building. It was a building called Vranica because it had been built by the Vranica construction company in Stjepan Radica Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what was the date when you joined the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It was in October, 1992. Whether the 15th or the 20th, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: At that time, do you know who the commander of the 4th Corps was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 4th Corps was Arif Pasalic. Later on, he was promoted to the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And who was your direct supervisor within the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic had several assistants. One of them was Sulejman Budakovic, chief of staff, and my unit was under him. My direct commander was Sulejman Budakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that you worked in the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown Exhibit 09413, and page 4 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: These three pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you identify those pictures for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Vranica building. This is the Vranica building too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how the 4th Corps came to occupy this building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, within the Vranica building itself, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Looking at the picture on the top, I was in the left-hand side of the building. The -- a detachment of the 41st Brigade was on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And which floor was that on?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The ground floor. That's where the offices were, and the communications centre was in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was there any other group or body that was occupying the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: At that time, I recall only that there was a court that was in the direction of the MUP. That was a bit further away from Stjepan Radic Street. Who else was there I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned that the 4th Corps was in the basement of the Vranica building. Do you know who occupied the floors above that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: There were civilian flats there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: The communications centre where you worked, was that the only communications centre under your control?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: This communications centre was under my direct control. All the other communications centres belonging to the brigades were under my remote control, but they had their own leaders who were responsible to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: After you joined the Bosnian army, did you continue living at home or did you move into army barracks?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. I lived at home. Most of the soldiers at that time lived at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And at that time, where was your home in relation to the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: If we look at this picture and draw a line in front of the building in this direction here, it was about a hundred or 150 metres away, on the same side. That's where my apartment block was and my flat. It's parallel to this street, Stjepan Radica Street. The name of the street was Ante Suanica [phoen], and the next road crossing Ante Suanica Street is my street, the street of Husein Skabuna [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you see the Vranica building from your house?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: This is a huge building. I think it has ten or more floors, and it covers a large surface area, and it can be seen from many parts of town. However, in front of this building there are other high-rise buildings, and right in front of my building there was a building which had more than three floors, and my flat was on the third floor, so it was really impossible to see this building from my flat. My view was to the east, towards the river Neretva and the whole town.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Turning to the 9th of May, 1993, were you on duty on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. On the 9th of May I was supposed to be on duty at 8.00, but I was prevented by an attack which began at 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Where was the attack?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It was a frontal attack on the entire town, or at least a whole part of town, the part of town with a majority Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what prevented you from going to your work at the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was prevented by the situation, the shelling, the bullets, the soldiers milling around who were not wearing insignia. I had insignia, but they didn't. And it was clear to me that I had to report somewhere else, because the place where I was supposed to report at 8.00, well, nothing would be happening there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Which place were you supposed to report to at 8.00?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to report to the command of the 4th Corps and take over the duty of duty officer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And that was where exactly?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The command was in the building we showed here, the Vranica building. My office was on the ground floor, which you can see here. The centre was below that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was that building being attacked?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The building was being attacked very fiercely, and all the flats above the offices had been gutted. I think you -- they're still gutted. It was attacked very fiercely.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How could you see this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it with my own eyes, but my wife was able to leave the flat at that time, and she told me not to go there. I went downstairs as far as the entrance to the building I lived in, and I saw there was chaos in that direction and that it would have been crazy to attempt to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you say there was chaos, can you describe what you mean by "chaos."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: When I say "chaos," in this case I mean very heavy shelling of the building on the west part of the river Neretva, which is still under the control of the majority population, the Croats, and this was a building in which there were Bosniaks. All the other buildings were spared that attack. Only this building was being fiercely attacked, both by infantry and artillery. In front of my building there was chaos because there were large numbers of people, both soldiers and civilians, who didn't know where to go and what to do. So the soldiers probably had particular assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Which army were those soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: These soldiers were HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how could you tell that they were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Only on the basis of the badges they wore on their left shoulder, and also by their accents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to describe the badges that they wore on their left shoulder?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Not in detail because I haven't seen it since that time, but I know there was a chequerboard coat of arms and big letters HVO. I think above that it said in small letters Croatian Defence Council, but I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, turning to the people from the 4th Corps, on the night of the 8th of May, how many people were on duty in the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: In the Vranica building, in the course of a night, there would never be more than 20 or 30 people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. I'm sorry for interrupting. After a question that was put to you, you answered but Madam Prosecutor did not pick up on one of these items. You mentioned that these were HVO soldiers because of the badges they were wearing and because of their accents. What did you mean to say when you said that their accent was different to yours? Have you understood my question? Would you like me to repeat it? You mentioned -- you mentioned that these soldiers had an accent. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for me, it means that we in Mostar can tell who is not from Mostar. People who come from 20 kilometres away are not Mostar locals, and we can tell that by their accents, and especially so if they come from a hundred or 120 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these soldiers did not come from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can I -- in the same direction. Would you then say that all the ABiH soldiers that were engaged in Mostar were actually from Mostar? There were no soldiers on the Muslim side which came from outside Mostar. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the HVO soldiers I mentioned, of course they were not all from outside. 90 per cent of them were from Mostar. But the voices I heard, I recognised them as non-Mostar locals. The same goes for the BH army. 90 per cent were local people from Mostar, but there were also others. All those who felt that Mostar should be defended from the aggression came and joined us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, you were explaining to the Court that during night duty there would never be more than 20 to 30 persons on duty at any one time. On the night of the 8th of May, were there 20 to 30 people on duty on that night?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That night the situation was the same. There were probably 25 to 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were those people all belonging to the 4th Corps or were those people from other brigades or corps?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I said that in this building, when you look at the left-hand side as in this picture, the 4th Corps was on the left-hand side, whereas the 41st Brigade was on the right-hand side. So if you add up the soldiers from both brigades, there might have been about 30 in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the accused are not receiving interpretation into a language they understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter, what is happening in the interpretation booth? I cannot hear the translation. It's fine now. Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were those people, the 20 to 30 that you have described, all belonging to the 4th Corps, or were these people from other brigades or other corps?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: There was nobody else from other corps. This was the 4th Corps, which had a number of brigades, one of which was the 41st Motorised Brigade, which was headquartered in that building. So the total of people in both of these buildings, both of the brigade and of the corps, could -- could have been 30 to 35, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those soldiers who were on duty on the 8th of May, the night of the 8th of May going into the morning of the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say that there were 30 soldiers there, and I didn't see what happened to any one of them, however, I heard of the fate that befell many of them. Some of them managed to change into civilian clothes and flee from that building. As for others who were caught, some of them were shot on the spot, and some of them were taken to the building of the school of mechanical engineering where they met their end.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 08588.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe I'm anticipating, but I would like to know how you know that some of the soldiers were shot on the spot. Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that I didn't see any of this with my own eyes. I told you that I didn't see what happened to them myself, however I heard about it. But what one normally hears under those circumstances is usually true. Very seldom is there any misinformation under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 08551.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, if you could take a look at the exhibit that is on the screen in front of you, and you see that there is a list of names. You see that there is a list of names on the exhibit. Do you recognise any of those names?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I know many names, but there's a name that I'm familiar with that's missing from the list, that of Juskovic. In those days, and particularly later, there was a videotape showing their arrest. It was frequently shown on TV of Mostar, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and probably in the wider region. Following that broadcast of that programme, of that tape, nobody ever saw those people again. As for the story that I heard, I believe it to be fully true because there was very little misinformation at the time. And soon thereafter, after these people were arrested, they were killed at the school of mechanical engineering, or someplace else, but very soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: The persons named on this list, are these people who you knew from your work?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Under number 10, Penava Fahir, son of Halil, was in the Signals Unit of the 41st Brigade. I knew him personally. As for the others, I used to come across them inside the building, outside of the building, but I didn't get into a conversation with them. They were junior in relation to me in terms of their rank, and also younger than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. Mr. Saric, could you please repeat the name of the person under 10 whom apparently you knew because he was in the Signals Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're having problems again. It seems that we have B/C/S interpretation in the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Saric, you told us just a bit ago that you knew somebody, you knew the person under number 10. Could you please give us the name of that person again, the person who was in the Signals Unit, in the communications unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fahir Penava.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, after the attack on the 9th of May, did the Bosnian army, the 4th Corps, continue to use the Vranica building as its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It is clear that the 4th Corps had more than 30 people. There were 30 people in the building at the time of the attack. Everybody else was elsewhere. Some of them were in their homes. However, a large number of soldiers and military leaders were on the left side, on the left bank, where they remained after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: As far as the Vranica building itself is concerned, after the 9th of May, did the soldiers in the 4th Corps continue to use that building as a place of work?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't think that anybody came. I didn't, and I assume that others didn't either. I assume nobody came there to work, because that place was the one that was destroyed the most. So people wouldn't come there. As for the information, the information is normally passed within seconds, and we would learn that this is not located there any longer but, rather, elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what was then the new location of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: There were a number of facilities that were used for the army at the time. As for the command of the 4th Corps, if you have in mind the commander and his assistants, then that was located in the building of Energopetrol, which was a residential building. On the ground floor there were some shops. And next to that building is the building of Energopetrol, which is quite a dominant structure, as a result of which that whole neighbourhood was called Energopetrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall the date on which these premises started to be used by the Bosnian army, the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned that after the attack on the 9th of May you did not continue going to work. What did you do following -- in the days following the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The situation in general after the 9th of May was very difficult, especially for those who were persecuted at the time. I considered myself to be persecuted at the time because I belonged to an army which wasn't on its home terrain, so to speak, so I had to hide. I was unable to leave town. I had to go into hiding, and I did that until the July -- the 7th of July of 1993, which means that this involved two months of successful hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Where did you hide?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was hiding mostly with Croats whom I considered to be friends. I'm friends with these people to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was this in Mostar or did you leave the city?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: All of this was taking place in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to say where in Mostar you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Initially I hid in the buildings in the vicinity of my apartment, and later on in the part of the town called Ilic, where a long time ago my ancestors had their estate. My father hailed from that area, and I went to stay with the people who had purchased that estate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Whereabouts is Ilici in relation to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: This is an area to the west on the banks of the Radobolje river, on both banks of that river. In the foothills is the source of that river, which has its source there, and flows into the Neretva River near Mostar. That entire area is known as Ilici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: When did you go to Ilici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but sometime in late May, towards the end of May, because I know that I listened to the news of the 30th of June in Ilici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned the date of the 7th of July earlier, saying that you had to go into hiding and did so until the 7th of July, 1993. What happened on the 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: What was quite unusual that day is that I took a nap in the afternoon. They woke me up --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I could just stop you briefly. I apologise for interrupting. Where were you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: What do you mean where? You mean where in the building or where in Ilici?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Both; whereabouts in Ilici, and in which building in Ilici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: In Ilici that was an area next to the Radobolje river where there is a famous place called Londza where the estate of Sarici was, and this building is almost immediately next to the current regional hospital of Mostar. This is the family house of the man who had purchased this land from my mother. He built that house there where I was hiding. The house had a ground floor with a garage and a workshop, then it had the first floor with living-room, some rooms, kitchen and so on, and then an attic above it which at the time was not in use. I was staying on the floor which was in use by the family, and my room was facing the hospital, which means it was facing north, and it was the door of this room that on the 7th of July they knocked on. The man who took me in was knocking on the door and there were two soldiers with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were taking a nap to begin with and that you were woken up. What time of day was this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It was at 4.00 in the afternoon, about that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What caused you to wake up?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The knocking on the door and the calling of my name. The man in whose house I was staying called out my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What did you do when you heard your name being called and the knock on the door?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I put my trousers on and opened the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What happened when you opened the door?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: When I opened the door, I saw two armed soldiers standing behind the man. They came in in quite a rough manner and started searching the room. As they were searching, they found some jewellery which I had hidden and which belonged to my wife, and they took it in quite a selfish manner, as though they were hiding it from each other. And then they also took some cash that I had in my bag. They searched the whole room and the bed where I slept, and they found an automatic rifle belonging to the man in whose house I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What were the men wearing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The soldiers wore uniforms, and at the time everybody had the same uniforms - those were camouflage uniforms - and the only thing that differed were the badges on their sleeves. Their badge was that of the HVO. I knew one of the soldiers. He was Franjo Cvitkovic from Citluk. He used to live in Mostar before the war. I don't know how long he had lived there before the war. I just knew him as a resident of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: So after they searched the property and found some jewellery, what happened?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was taken to a jeep which was parked in front of the door. We got into the jeep, and we drove past Londza, the house of my parents, and then we went to the olive grove. That is to say we went straight to the school of mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What happened when you got to the school of mechanical engineering?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: When I came to the school of mechanical engineering, they took me to the basement and shut me in a room where there were already 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 09413, please. And page 11 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the pensioners' centre, and then underneath is the Mostar hotel. The photograph on the top resembles it, but I don't think it is. As for the bottom one, it's definitely not that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could we turn to page 12, please. Do you recognise either of these two photographs?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The bottom one. The bottom one, and the upper one, the right corner. Yes, that's what it is. This -- this -- this right portion on the upper photograph resembles it, but I don't think that this is the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned you were taken to a room when you arrived at the mechanical faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to be shown this document, please, and a copy to be placed on the ELMO. Sorry, there are two sketches, one of which I'm going to get to later. I believe the witness has a different sketch. If I can just take a look and I can show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could our learned friend please tell us who produced this map. We don't see any ERN number, nor is this document on the list of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: My learned friend for the Defence is quite right. There is no ERN on the document, and I'm about to ask the witness some questions about this document in order to identify the document, and the explanation will then be forthcoming as to why the Defence are only receiving this document this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, could you identify the document that has been placed before you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. To the right you can see the basement of the school of mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before we get into the detail of the document, just to ask you where this document has come from.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: What we are discussing now was taking place in 1993. It's 2006 now, which is to say that it's been 13 years since I last saw this -- these premises. I tried to recall it, and I drew this yesterday, last night, and of course I was relying on my memories, but you have to take into account that it's been 13 years, and 13 years which I was doing my best to forget at that, so it's possible that all not all of the details are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I hope that answers my learned friend's question as to where this document has come from, and I'd ask that the document be given an In Court Exhibit number. That will be 00027.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct. It will be IC 00-0027.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saric, you explained that you arrived at the mechanical faculty. Are you able to describe where you were taken to, with the use of the sketch diagram if that assists you at all in your recollections.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can see what I'm pointing to now, but the entrance door, which is right next to the stairs, is the door facing the street, the street with the trees. As you enter through the front door, to the right there are stairs leading to the basement, and to the left are stairs leading to the ground floor which is a bit above the ground. And then there are these two rooms where I stayed when they brought me there, but this was after the events which took place in the premises on the right. So they took me straight to these stairs on the right and then straight to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but if -- if any of this detail matters at all to the Prosecution, it's very difficult for us to follow because we're not able to see what the witness is referring to, and I wonder whether it might be possible for the Prosecution to devise some way to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: My apologies, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The document is now on the ELMO so everyone can see it. Could you please use a pointer, a pencil, and could you show us what you mean on the document itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we compare the picture underneath, this is the floor plan of the building. Here is the entrance, and in front of it are the pine trees shown in this picture. That's the street leading towards the interior of the university. And I was taken down these stairs here and taken to this cell. There were some 15 or 16 people in this cell already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saric, please speak into the microphone. The interpreters can't hear you otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was taken down these stairs straight to this cell. In this cell there were about 15 people already. The cell next door was empty, and in this one there were three or four people. I don't know because we were locked in. This is a wooden lattice, the sort that is usual in basements so air would come in through that. This big room here was used as the toilet. All those who passed through the faculty of mechanical engineering, not as students but as victims, went to the toilet here. This was never cleaned. Nobody ever cleaned this. This area labelled A was the room where they tortured prisoners, where they beat them up, whereas B was used for executions. It was used for killing. This was the famous slaughterhouse. This was the torture chamber, and this was the slaughterhouse. This was the audience, observing what would happen to them while those who were completely out of favour were taken to B. I remained in the cell, and fortunately, I survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, just to go through in some more detail. You've given a lot of information there, and we'll go through in more detail the descriptions that you've begin. Taking, first of all, the room to you which you were put into when you arrived at the mechanical faculty. You mentioned the number of people that were in the cell. Can you describe the room; how big it was, whether there were any windows, any furniture, whether it was clean or dirty, the sleeping facilities, food and water.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, no cleaners had been there for years. No one had ordered the prisoners to clean it for years. It was probably the dirtiest place where people lived at that time. I spent three very difficult days there. Throughout those three days I was given no food and no water.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How big was the room?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The room was very small. In my estimation today, then, it was -- well, today it's probably different the way I remember it from -- well, it was 2.5 or -- metres or 2.80 metres wide and about 3 metres long. So let's say 2.5 metres by 3 metres, or maybe 2.70 by 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What about the conditions for sleeping?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The window was covered with bricks from the outside so that very little light came in, although there was a little daylight, which was very good. This was the wooden lattice door, and there was a board that was placed against it. The floor was covered only with pieces of broken furniture, a cupboard door, things like that. And there was a small chair. The size was that of a chair for a school child, and whoever managed to sit down was very happy. The others had to lie on those boards or sit or squat. You couldn't lie down and fall asleep. People slept in a squatting or sitting position. Those who managed to sit down had the chance of dozing off for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: The 15 persons that you've mentioned as being in the room, do you know what ethnicities they were?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: All the people I knew were Bosniaks, and from what the others were saying, all the others were Bosniaks too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were these people male or female?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: They were all male. There were no women there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were they military or civilian people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: All the ones I knew, they were all civilians. I was the only one who was a "military person."

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what ages were the people in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: They were mostly aged between 40 and 50. There was an elderly man and also a young man who was about 20. He may have been the son of the man I said was called Djukic, who had gone to the mechanical engineering school. I had gone to the electrical engineering school. And his son was held there for three days. All the others were aged between 40 and 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you know anything of these people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I knew a few of them. This man Djukic, whom I knew from school. There was Mustafa Pilatovac, an electrical engineer; then there was Stupac, I can't recall his first name; then Hasan Trcalo, who had also gone to school with me, to primary school. I can't recall any other names now, but I'm certain I know these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you able to see if there were -- there was anybody guarding the door to the room where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No, because if there had been a guard there, he would have been punished like us. As the conditions were so horrible, no guard wanted to be there unless he was being punished. The guards were up here, either at the gate, at the door, or in this corridor here. As all the windows were blocked, there were probably soldiers outside, guards outside, but none of the guards spent any time in the basement except for the time it took to torture or kill someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: On that first day that you spent at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. May interrupt to ask an additional question on the conditions in detention. Were you allowed to use the toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was the toilet here. It was public and open. Everyone here used it. It was never washed. It was just a room. There was no sewage. There was no water. It was just a room where people went to do what they had to do there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Following on from Your Honour's question, how did you get from the cell to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: This part of the cell was closed with a wooden lattice, and it was facing the stairway. Those who needed to go to the toilet, and those were very few - as I told you, I had spent three days without food or water so there was no need to go - but those who needed to go would call a guard, and they would perhaps have to yell for about 20 minutes before a guard would come, and he would just open this gate, take away the board, and he would say, "Okay, go," and they would close the door and go upstairs again, and then he would come back a minute or two later to lift the board and put the man back in again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it -- I'm sorry. Is it correct to assume that there was a rather unpleasant smell in that cellar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was terrible. "Terrible" is an understatement. It was ten times terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: On the first day that you were at the mechanical faculty, you've explained you arrived and you were put in the cell. Did you remain in the cell throughout that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Not the whole day. After an hour, half an hour - I can't be sure - they took me for interrogation. I was brought to this room here. This is the desk and the chair on which I sat.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And from the diagram, is that room on a different floor from the cell that you were contained in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, I've drawn a thin line here, a slight line, to show that the right-hand side was in the basement. The left-hand side was raised. It was a mezzanine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was there anybody with you in that room where you've shown you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Here? In this room there was no one. Occasionally soldiers would go in and out. There were three doors, and they would go in and out in order to confuse and intimidate me. So they would go here and here and here, but they would all just pass through.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did anybody speak to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Only the commander of the military police, who came in through this door. His name was Dzidic, also known as Dzida. He opened this door and saw me here, and he made a sarcastic comment. He said, "What's up, Chief?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saric, you've just told us that the commander of the military police was called Dzidic, nicknamed Dzida. Is that the person who was prosecuted in a case in which you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this was not the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are telling us that the commander of the military police was called Dzidic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I only heard this. What his real position was, who the real commander was, who issued the orders, I don't know, but people said that Dzida was the chief of police. Of course, the overall chief of police, the main one, was someone else. But in my view, Dzida, as far as I knew, was the chief of police in that building where I was being held, the faculty of mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: In the room where you saw Dzidic, how long did you remain in that room?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what did you do during that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I had a pen and paper, and I was supposed to describe the events that had happened from the beginning of the war until the point when I arrived in that building. It was supposed to be a kind of statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And who asked you to make that statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. One of the soldiers who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you make a statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I did, in pencil, in my own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: After finishing the statement, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: From this room I was taken straight back to the cell in the basement. It was around 9.00 in the evening. It was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: By whom were you taken back to the cell?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The HVO soldier who was there on duty that day. I don't know what his name is or who he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you got back to the cell at 9.00 that night, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I tried to get some sleep. I tried to forget about all this, as if it wasn't happening, but of course I couldn't do that. I didn't fall asleep all that night. I was afraid for my family, and also I heard moans coming from this cell here. There were three or four men in that cell. And when there were no guards around, we would call out to each other from one cell to the next, and so we learned that they came from Konjic municipality and that that evening or the previous evening they had been caught by HVO soldiers in the area of Salakovac and that they had been brought to prison here. One of them, who I think was the youngest and the strongest of them, managed to come to the door of our cell, asking for water, and then he told us the details. He said that the person who was moaning, that his name was Hebibovic, or he said that they had already killed Hebibovic. They kept saying, They killed Hebibovic. Whether it was the man who was moaning or somebody who had already been killed before, I'm not sure, but we thought Hebibovic was the man lying on the floor there. And this Hebibovic, if that was him, took a long time to die. He must have been very strong. We heard him moaning all night, and then it stopped at around 5.00 or 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You've mentioned that he was lying down. Is this something that you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes only on the following day when I was going to the toilet. I was unable to relieve myself and I went back, and I saw him then. There was a mess here, and he was lying in the middle of that mess.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 08534.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: As you'll see, the copy of this document is not very clear, but are you able to identify this document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, I hate to interrupt, but my learned friend did say that it was a poor copy. When we received it, it was a poor copy. We tried to look at it in our office under various kinds of light, but it's not just a poor copy, but the first and last name of the person who -- whose death certificate this purports to be is missing. So this document cannot be used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response to my learned friend's remarks, Your Honour can see that lower down on the document the last and first names of the parents are legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. The names of parents need not mean anything. They could have had 15 children. This happens in Bosnia. Or it could be another family called Hebibovic. There is no first and last name. This is precisely why in the countries of the former Yugoslavia death certificates look like this, to identify the person. We need his first and last name, his date of birth and death, and also his parents' names. Let the OTP show the parents' birth certificates and marriage certificates and then we might conclude that this person might be their son, but this is not evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have to be quick. We only have five minutes left now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question to the witness, hopefully addressing the remarks of my learned friend, would be regarding those parents of the man that he witnessed to be dead in detention and whether he knows who those people are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know those people, although I do know the family. It's a family from Glavaticevo above the Boracko lake near Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you knew Mr. Ahmet Hebibovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you've just said -- spoken to the contrary. Which family are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking of the Hebibovic family, but that is a large family that has been there for generations. So the last name comes from that area. I know, for example, a journalist whose last name is Hebibovic who works in Mostar, but there are Hebibovics who do not know each other. The family is very large.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document was issued by Konjic municipality. You can see the number and the date here. The office still exists in Konjic, so instead of looking at illegible copies, the OTP has its office in Mostar, let them go to Konjic. These are public registers. They're open to the public. Let them get a valid death certificate and then we can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can short circuit matters. We are going to try and obtain the best copies that we can get a hold of, if that assists any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have another question with regard to this document. The events that the witness speaks about cannot have taken part before the 7th of July. Actually, it must be the 8th of July that a person the witness says was named Hebibovic died in the technical faculty. However, on this document, date, month, year and hour of death one can read a 6 and then a 7, which would refer to the month, perhaps, and that would mean that the document predates the events the witness is speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that Mr. Saric may be able to assist in that regard if he's given the opportunity to answer a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, would you be able to assist in that discrepancy in the date, the events you describe having taken place on the night of the 7th into the morning of the 8th of July and the death certificate, as His Honour pointed out, being dated the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way this question is put seems to me to be unacceptable, because we do not know whether the certificate refers to that person at all. Therefore, information as to whether he died on the 6th or the 7th is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are many more essential questions we can put in this case, so I shall ask a question now. The person you saw lying on the ground and moaning all night, the person whom you saw in the early hours of the morning, you realised that this person was dead. Could you tell us, please, what the surname and Christian name of this person was, if you knew it at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The man who died, his last name was Hebibovic. I learned that from the man who was with him, who had been taken prisoner with him and who had been in the cell with him. He came to the door of our cell and told us that this man's name was Hebibovic and that he was finished. I didn't know the man personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The man whom you spoke to told you that they had been captured in Konjic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, near Salakovac, near Dreznica. Between Dreznica and Salakovac. That's 30 kilometres away from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this person named Hebibovic, was he a civilian or a soldier from the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were civilians. They were on their way to trade. These were people who tried to survive in that area and to get something for their families, whether to buy something or smuggle something, I don't know, and they were brought in as civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It is now 10.30. For technical reasons we have to have a break now. I'd like to remind the Prosecution that it had told us that it needed two hours. Theoretically you have half an hour left. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're resuming the hearing. The Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, without taking up any more time on this issue of the death certificate, the Prosecution has found the copy of the original that was sent to us as the result of a request for assistance from the government, and I believe it is somewhat a trick of the light, but if you hold it in the right light you can make out the name of the person on the face of the certificate. If Your Honour would like to take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I object to this procedure as well. The first reason is for practical purposes, because this document is supposed to be entered into e-court if it is admitted. In the e-court system, none of us will be able to hold this document up to the light and study it carefully under the light. The second reason is that we don't have to be extra tolerant, because this is not a document that came from various archives. No. This is a document that came from the public source, public registry books. As my learned friend said, they received a copy of it, so obviously it shouldn't be a problem to receive another certified copy from the municipality, because the photocopying of such documents is complicated. This is how they protect it from forgery. So I think that they need to mail us a new copy from Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We shall rule on this objection at a later time. You may now continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, in connection with the events that you were describing in the mechanical faculty and, in particular, with Hebibovic and that incident that you described, I have one further exhibit in connection with that that I would like the witness to be shown, and that is Exhibit 03249. On the B/C/S version of that document it is page 1. It's just a single-page document of the B/C/S version. Page 2 of the English translation thereof. Mr. Saric, could I ask you to look about halfway down that page, and if you could read out the paragraph that starts, "Pozorno patrolna sluzba." Mr. Saric, are you able to see the document that I've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this whole line of questioning on which we've now spent a considerable time. The witness's only information about this whole episode is apparently what he was told by somebody else. There is -- there is no evidence whatsoever to link any particular Hebibovic to the man who died in these unfortunate circumstances. And furthermore, Your Honour, for the witness to be shown this particular document which he -- he's not even been asked to recognise it or to whether he can authenticate it, is in violation of the Court's order for admission of evidence of the 13th of July, 2006, in which Your Honours have said that in general a document will not be admitted unless a witness is able to provide some information about it. So I object to this whole line of questioning on this episode.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard what you had to say, Mr. Murphy. The only thing I see that can be achieved by your question is that there is a report here whereby they're informing that 10 people were taken into custody, among them Hebibovic. So the question that needs to be put is this: Among the people who are listed here, are there any persons whom the witness knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of these 10 names, I knew --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's currently employed in the Mostar television --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- company. And as for Adem Hebibovic, I heard of him. The man that I know is Salih Sijamija, number 10. I know him personally. As for Adem Hebibovic, I just read out his name here, and I remember that he's precisely the person mentioned at the time. Adem was mentioned at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You just mentioned Salih Sijamija. Please tell us, did you see this person in detention while you were there, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't see him, however I know him and I saw him after the war. He survived all of these terrible atrocities, and as I told you, he's currently employed at the Mostar television station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this person that you saw before, you said that that person was in detention in the faculty of mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Adem Hebibovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what about Sijamija? Was he detained there as well or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at the time while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, you've mentioned previously that you spent three days at the mechanical faculty. What happened and where did you go on that third day at the mechanical faculty?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: On the third day there was another interrogation before the investigative organs of SIS. That was once again at around 10.00 in the morning. This interrogation took a couple of hours. It maybe went on until 1.00. Following that, I was taken under escort to the prison at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you return to the room in which you were being held at the mechanical faculty after this interrogation on the third day?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Once they came to fetch me and take me to interrogation, everybody else remained in the room. Upon my return, I found an empty room. There was nobody in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know where those people went?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know at the time. Later on I learned that all of them went to Heliodrom. I even saw some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you've said that you were taken to Heliodrom on that day. Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was taken by the military police, military police patrol. We travelled in a jeep; two soldiers and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Heliodrom, what happened?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: One of the soldiers escorting me had taken papers from the faculty of mechanical engineering. They had been prepared in advance. And he handed them over to the guard who opened the door. They didn't come inside with me. The three of them went back in a jeep, and I entered the Heliodrom building on my own. Based on the papers that the guard received, I was sent immediately to the basement, to the area where there were solitary confinement cells.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Once again, I wonder -- there is a second sketch that I distributed earlier entitled "Prison Heliodrom." I wonder if that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, before we begin with any detail on this document, as with the previous sketch from the mechanical faculty, could you tell us where this document has come from and identify it for us.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I drew this sketch as well last night, also relying on my memory, and I can see that dimensions are not to scale. These empty rooms here were not in use, so it's possible that proportions are not quite accurate or clear. I drew this based on my memory and my experiences there because, after all, I spent eight months in these surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, turning to your previous evidence that you were taken to the basement in Heliodrom, if it assists in using the sketch then do so, but could you describe where exactly you were taken to.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: This is the sketch of the basement of the prison. From the entrance gate one enters a hallway, and then there are stairs leading downstairs which take you to this three-part metal gate, which is as high as this wall. That is to say it is about 1 metre below the ceiling, so that there was this opening of 1 metre through which air and light came in. Through that gate, once we passed it, we went into this area here. I can't tell you now with full certainty whether there were only three cells here. There may have been four or five. However, these cells were separated with this wall, and there was an opening here without a door, just an opening. And I was taken to the cell on the left. Regardless of how many cells there were, I was in the one that was on the far left, number 1. And I spent there from the 10th of July to the 20th of July, and this is where I saw Habibi. This room was 2 by 2.5. It had a window, it had natural light, so at first glance it didn't resemble a solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you alone in the cell?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. There was a person there, Idris Habibija, whom I found when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions in the cell relating to sanitation, whether you received food and water, and the sleeping facilities.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: These 10 days is a very brief period of time when compared to the entire stay there. My first impression upon arriving in cell number 1 was this: I saw just one bed there. It had nothing on it except for blankets. On the following day after my arrival, they took the bed out. There was just a concrete floor and nothing else. We had several blankets on that floor. We would place them underneath us and also cover ourselves with blankets, although there was no need for that because it was summertime and we didn't need many blankets then. There was a bucket, an ordinary tin bucket, where we relieved ourselves. Every week or so the bucket was emptied by the users of this toilet, and it was taken to the toilet facilities that were shared in these premises, which were at the end of this corridor. The corridor was about 30 metres long, and at the end of it was this toilet. We had five minutes' time to empty the bucket and to wash ourselves, and then we had to be back. This cell was dry. It was summertime, and the walls were filthy. The concrete floor was all scratched. It wasn't new. But in relation to what I experienced later, here and here, the difference was quite dramatic, because this cell had daylight. It had a window, and the window was not closed. This is as far as cell number 1 is concerned. As you can see based on the dates, I left cell number 1 on the 20th of July, and I stayed in cell number 2 until the 25th of February. So that was the longest that I spent in a cell. This window in this cell was all walled up. The wall in front of the cell and the gate did not permit for any light to pass through. Only just a little bit of light would pass, so that in the lightest of days it was quite dark in there. There was one light bulb here and here in the corridor. If in the middle of the day the light went off, we didn't know in our cell whether it was day or night. That is to say it was completely dark there. This cell was very dirty, too, because it must have been used previously. However, there were military-type mattresses on the floor, and there was seven of us in this cell. There was no space for walking, because the width of this cell was 2 metres. So when seven people lie down, one could only jump over the bodies. That is to say there was no opportunity for us to walk in the cell. The guards would regularly bring, in the morning and in the afternoon, some food. In the morning it would be tea and a piece of bread, slice of bread, and in the afternoon cooked meals. I see many people whom I knew from before and who stayed there with me. And throughout my stay there, until the 19th of April, I observed that a lot of them had lost a great deal of weight. They were walking skeletons. Many of them were wounded, black and blue, experienced great suffering. This was basically a terrible prison, and all it lacked was a gas chamber and then the picture would have been complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How long did you spend in this second cell?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: You can see here that I was in cell number 2 from the 20th of July to the 25th of February. It could have been the 24th of February, I'm not fully certain, but about five months -- more than five months.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And during your daily routine within these first two cells that you've mentioned, did you leave the cell at any time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Listen, it was absolutely impossible. We could go for a walk just once a week, and that was on our way to the toilet and back, and we actually had to run. That was all the walking we received. And there were seven of us in this cell. So the time needed to go to the toilet and get ourselves ready for the following week was a very brief time indeed. As I said to you, it was once a week and always in the morning when there was nobody else there, because later on the prisoners from other floors would arrive. So before they came down the stairway to the cafeteria or to the dining hall which was here, that was the time we had available for us to rush to these toilets.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And just to clarify, what year were these events taking place in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: This was in 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: After you were in cell number 2, where were you moved to then and what were the conditions?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: From cell number 2 I was transferred to cell number 3. The conditions were identical, although this cell was significantly larger; at least, so it seemed to me, because I was alone in that cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop, Mr. Saric. Mr. Praljak was on his feet, but please go ahead. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May I be excused, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But we can continue without his presence, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. Very well. Thus we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, you were in the process of describing your transfer to cell number 3 and stating that the conditions were identical although it was significantly larger. If you'd like to continue your description from there.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I drew it as a larger cell but it's possible that it seemed larger to me only because I was there alone. I was there alone for about one month and then they brought in another prisoner, Enver Cibo, and we spent some ten days together, maybe less. The general conditions, as I have said, were identical, and our daily routine was also identical, which is to say that once a week we went on our toilet round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but something doesn't add up. The witness has said that he was alone for one month and then another inmate was put in the same cell and they were together for another ten days. That adds up to much more than a month. But he has also indicated that he has been in this cell all and all for one month. So I would be grateful for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Saric --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It's possible that it was during the last week. It's very hard for me now to pinpoint the dates. I'm fully sure only about the first date and the last date, that is to say the 10th of July and the 19th of April. What happened in between is all approximate. But he stayed with me for a week. So as I was analysing this sketch, I wrote that it was a total of one month that I stayed in this cell, including the time I stayed with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what happened after this period of time that you spent with -- I think you mentioned his name was Cibo. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Nothing remarkable happened during that month or during the time when I was with him, but what was remarkable is that when I arrived there by myself there was an iron gate there with bars, and what was interesting was that this door was covered with a kind of a plywood, and there was a hole punched through the plywood, and so through that hole I was able to observe how people passed to the dining hall to have their meals. I could see them going there and coming back. So through this plywood I would also speak to them, and they would look into my cell and I would look at them through the hole. Sometimes they would pass a book to me or some cigarettes so that this cell was quite a refreshment for me given that I had spent the previous five months without any kind of support. The support that I received in cell number 3 gave me hope that something better would happen. And then Cibo joined me, and then we spent some five to seven days together during which nothing remarkable happened. The good thing about cell number 3 was that it was bathed in light. It had sufficient light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I failed to get the whole picture. You said that your contact with the hall was through a peephole sort of, and then you said that you received books. Did the books fit through that hole or did the guards assist you in getting the books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can imagine a plywood on the door with a hole through which I was able to look. This plywood was attached with a wire and some flexible plastic wiring, so there was a space of some 5 centimetres through which one could pass a book to me. I think that it took me only one day to read a very long book because there was nothing else for me to do. So the plywood could be moved, could be moved for bit -- for some 5 centimetres, so something small could be passed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: During your time, did you come into contact with any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. The guards would come and do their job. They would mostly inquire as to any property we may have had outside. They probably had their plans about it. And then they would put questions to us, "What did you do before? Were you a soldier or not?" and similar questions, and they would mostly try to provoke some individuals who -- not that they allowed it but were susceptible. There was, for example, Mustafa Hadrovic there, who used to work as a reserve policeman when the war broke out, and they particularly insulted and tortured him. I think that life was very, very hard for him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How do you know that this was taking place with Mr. Hadrovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, he had been with me in room number 2. A guard would come and call out his name. He would ask him to come out. When he went out, the guard would take him off somewhere. On his return, he would be all black and blue or bloody. He would be frightened. There would be swearing, cursing, threats. He was very badly maltreated during his absences, but they would bring him back to the same cell. He didn't go anywhere else. And then he would tell us what happened to him, who had done that to him and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, before these events I didn't know any of them, but later on I found out some names. There was Zeljko Marjanovic, for example, whom I may have mentioned, and he had been a guard at the faculty of mechanical engineering while I was there. And there was a man called Nikola. And the shift leader and the one who did the most provoking, I would recognise his name if I heard it now. Later on he became either the mayor or deputy mayor of a municipality in Mostar. A very bad man. I didn't know any of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the Heliodrom was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, in my view the commander was light-years away. The only contact I had was with the guards. That was the level of contact I had. But we did hear, in conversations, and when we went to the toilet there would always be somebody coming out of this room here, and rumours spread very quickly. We learned a lot, but it was all hearsay, not evidence. I only know that there was a certain Smiljanic who was responsible for that camp, but who that man is, what he looks like, I don't know, I never saw him. They mentioned someone called Pusic, but these were all people who were very far removed from the ordinary prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
