utterances.text: I would like to come back to the events you have described regarding Mr. Hadrovic. Him you mentioned, you said he had been ill-treated. Have you said that as an example? Were there others who were similarly treated, or was he, in your recollection, the only one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the only one who -- who didn't suffer too much. All the others were terribly injured and suffered terribly. In cell 3 I saw people who were worse off every day. They lost a lot of weight. I was one of those who lost a lot of weight also. I had always been over a hundred kilogrammes in weight, and then my weight fell to 70. Those people who came from the floor above looked terrible, those who came downstairs to eat. There were people who went missing. I would see them one day and not the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My question is a bit more specific. Have you witnessed other inmates being taken away and then coming back in a situation which made you believe that they had been ill-treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not witness the events taking place, but I would see someone one day and I would see him the next day, and I would see the difference. I would see wounds, bruises, and so on. There were people whom I saw simply wasting away, becoming living corpses. I saw people who were quite simply lost. I had had two colleagues who learned while they were there with me that their sons had been killed, and that was worse than anything physical that could have happened to them. The things people heard about their families was much worse than the physical mistreatment, which never stopped and which was never lacking. Very many people from upstairs were taken to the front lines as human shields, and that's where people were killed or injured. A man called Muharem Budic, who had been in my communications unit, lost his life while he was being used as a human shield on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. When Ms. Gillett, representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, put a question to you relating to the commander of the Heliodrom, you said of course that you were not in contact with the commander but that you had heard about a number of people like Mr. Smiljanic and a certain Mr. Pusic. Could you expand on this or could you talk more specifically about Mr. Pusic. Can you say anything more about these two people or is this all you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that Mr. Pusic often came, not to where we were but somewhere upstairs. All these were rumours. And that he kept promising a speedy release, a speedy exchange, but none of this ever transpired. He would arrive with false promises to calm people down. It was mostly false promises that he gave. That's what I know about him. But I never saw him in my life. I never had any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are more questions to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saric, have you spoken to Mr. Hadrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did he tell you what had happened to him more precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We spoke about this very often, both during the events and afterwards. To the best of my knowledge, nobody took him away with the intention of killing him, of eliminating him. Rather, the intention was to vent their spite, to humiliate him, to make him wash the floors. And when he finished washing the floor, he would have to start over again and wash the same floor again. If he so much as dared to raise his eyes, he would receive a blow. The blows were not fatal, they were meant simply to humiliate him and inflict pain on him. He was also told to sing songs to the guards. Of course he couldn't sing well, and when he sang out of tune he would be beaten. He was constantly mistreated in these ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add something to the question that has just been put to you. You have just told us that as far as Mr. Hadrovic is concerned you spoke to him about these events because you stayed with him in the cell for quite a long time. He told you -- or did he tell you that the behaviour towards him were directed at him personally by some of the guards that were not complying with the instructions given by the commanding officers, or was this widespread? What did Mr. Hadrovic tell you about ill-treatment? What did you feel about this kind of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadrovic is a very good example of the things that happened. I assume, and you will discover whether it was part of a system, a way of bringing to heel these who were disobedient, but he was the -- or, rather, he was not the only one who was treated this way. There were others of a similar mind-set, but nobody was punished in the same way. We all went out occasionally into this corridor and were beaten. We can't say that we were badly injured, but when somebody hits you on the back with a truncheon, or kicks you in the shins, or hits you in the kidneys, these are not things easily forgotten, and there was a lot of that. However, the things that happened to Hadrovic happened at least once a week, and he would come back with cuts and bruises and terribly frightened and terribly humiliated. He would be made to clean people's shoes, bring water, so on and so forth. I don't know why nobody else from my cell was made to do the same kind of things, but there may be people who would have rather been killed than do those things. He, however, allowed himself to be humiliated, which is probably why it happened again and again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there seems to be an error in the transcript. The witness -- I'm speaking of line 50.3. He said that Mr. Hadrovic was the only one who was taken out of the cell and maltreated, whereas the record says he was not the only one, that there were others. At the end of this whole section of the witness's testimony it's evident because he repeats that Hadrovic was the only one from the cell who was tortured in this way. I think this is a major error, so if it might be corrected. It can be checked, of course, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. I distinctly remember that the witness said what is here, and if you look, he then added and said that he himself was also taken out into the corridor and -- or into the hall and beaten. But there are two different sets of facts. This specific humiliation, as I understand the witness, was typical only for Hadrovic, but taken out -- being taken and beaten was more general. Did I -- would you agree, Witness? Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, completely. Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, I don't think the witness understood the matter at issue. The tape can be listened to. I think this is clear, but in line 13 he says, "I don't know why nobody else from my cell was made to do the same kind of things." And that is in line with what he said at the outset, but at the outset the "not" is erroneously inserted, because he said expressly - I was listening carefully to the original - he said, "Hadrovic was the only one from my cell who was treated in this way." But it's best to ask the witness directly, Your Honours. With all due respect, your question was too complex. I'm sure the witness did not understand it because there were two parts to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might just shortly ask. I'm not actually following which line my learned friend is referring to in the transcript. I believe he mentioned line 53 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saric. Were several prisoners taken from the cell and beaten and then brought back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but only in this area here. Only in this area in front of the cell. Mustafa Hadrovic, however, was taken who knows where. We heard that he was upstairs, and he would be brought back an hour or two later. Nobody else suffered the same fate as him. Other people were beaten but not taken upstairs and humiliated in front of others and so on. That was what I was constantly trying to say. I don't know how it's reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You said that you personally had also been beaten in that way in the hall. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can confirm it. I can't prove it, however, because the bruises are not there any more. This happened against this wall between these two doors. Two or three would be taken out and two or three soldiers would arrive and then they would exorcise themselves for about five minutes and then go away and we would be put back in the cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were, I think -- well, Prosecutor, you will have to wind things up shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am mindful of the time, and I only have a couple of more questions for this witness which should be taken very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, do you know why you were placed into these particular cells that you've been describing to us?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume because I was an officer in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that perhaps for reasons of exchange or other reasons I was supposed to be treated differently from the other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What was the total amount of time that you spent in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: About eight months. That's what I always think. But here it is: From the 7th -- yes, I never calculated this. I have been trying to forget this ever since.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall the exact date on which you were released?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The 19th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how did you come to be released?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: On that day everything was disbanded, the whole camp. At least the building I was in. There was more than one building, but the building I was in was emptied on that day. I had the honour to leave on the last truck, so I could see all the others leaving before me. At about 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon I was already a free man. This emptying of the camp lasted all day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can you give an estimate as to how many persons you saw leaving on that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, that's my personal assessment, but I think at least a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the questions I have for the Prosecution. I would just ask that the sketch diagram that's been placed on the ELMO and that the witness has been referring to in relation to the Heliodrom be given an In Court number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be IC 00-0028.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which other exhibit would you like to tender into evidence? I'm now turning to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the photographs that are exhibited, number 09413, and that would be pages 4, 11 and 12; Exhibit number 8588, Exhibit number 8534, and Exhibit number 3249. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't wish to tender Exhibit number 8534 -- no, sorry. Yes, it's in there. We shall rule on that. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My -- I object to that document in the form in which it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Chamber will rule on this matter now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought Mr. Kovacic would say it. I think P 03249 is not admissible because, after Mr. Peter Murphy's objection, the witness did not deal with this document any further. If you remember, it is a daily combat report from the Mostar military police, and the date is the 6th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate on this matter this afternoon. Now, as far as the cross-examination is concerned, have you agreed upon who will cross-examine the witness first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, quite honestly, we haven't been able to discuss the details, but according to what we did manage to discuss among ourselves, I believe that we will be able to adhere to the time, and we will go in the same order that we had before the recess, which means that I will be the first. However, Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Praljak has no questions for the witness because we have no direct connection with the events the witness is testifying about. However, by Your Honour's leave, knowing that the other Defence teams do not have a lot to ask, Mr. Praljak would like to use the presence of this witness, as he is a communications engineer. There is a fact which is quite important for us in order to understand the situation with regard to telephone communications in Bosnia at the time, so Mr. Praljak would like to ask him a few technical questions because he is the best educated in this respect, just to make use of the presence of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've listened to what my learned friend proposes to direct cross-examination for this witness, and it appears to be beyond the scope of the evidence covered in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may remind the Court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. [Interpretation] If I may remind Your Honours, in his earlier statements the witness did discuss this in some detail. We were, of course, preparing for the cross bearing in mind what the witness was said to testify to. At the beginning of today's examination, the witness did say he was the chief of communications in the 4th Corps command. In his CV, he did say that he was an electrical engineer and that he had worked in the post office. Therefore, he is sufficiently informed to say something on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist on the question that was raised by the Prosecution. Referring to whether the questions would be outside the scope of examination-in-chief, under Rule 90, subrule (H), cross-examination may also occur where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party. And clearly the questions which Mr. Praljak proposes would fall into that category. Furthermore, under the same Rule, Your Honour, subpart (iii), the Trial Chamber may, in the exercise of its discretion, permit inquiry into additional matters. It would seem to me that if we could avoid bringing the witness back as a party witness for one of the accused we would save time, and the proposed line of questioning does seem to fall within that Rule. So I would submit that the Prosecution's objection is not well taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, further to the point that I just raised, it is fair to say that in the chart that was submitted and filed with both the Chamber and the Defence, there was no mention of the witness giving any evidence relating to communications matter and the subject of his job, which was simply mentioned at the beginning of direct examination, that being his employment. As far as cross-examination is concerned relating to Rule 90 subparagraph (H), once again I fail to see the relevance that the Defence is raising in asking questions of this witness in relation to communications matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... speak for Mr. Praljak, but Your Honour, I think I can indicate the relevance of these questions quite -- perhaps Mr. Praljak would prefer to do it himself, he's indicated, Your Honour, so I'll defer to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall deliberate on the matter right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a -- the Judges don't all agree here. What is important is to understand how relevant this is. Mr. Praljak, those questions which you wish to put to the witness, how can they serve your interests? Because according to Rule 90(H) -- let me it out: "Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the evidence-in-chief ..." It seems that the Prosecution did not ask any questions pertaining to communications, and affecting the credibility of the witness does not apply. And this is where there might be a slot for the Defence: "... and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, to the subject-matter of that case." So in what ways are the questions which you're going to put going to be serving your interests? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The witnesses so far -- the journalist whose name I can't remember, spoke about how difficult it was to have telephone communication with other areas. Then there was a witness who was into karate, and he said that the HVO disallowed any telephone communication with Croatia. The entire system of communication between the armies so far was covered by the people --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] -- who were completely incompetent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me sum up and then I'll give the floor back to you. The Defence counsel is telling us that a number of witnesses has -- have talked about communication problems. I remember that this issue was addressed a number of times. This is why Mr. Praljak, who is an expert on the matter, would like to clarify a number of points. So this is the position adopted by the Defence. What do you have to say, Ms. Gillett, to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my first point and the reason I rose to my feet - apologies for interrupting Mr. Praljak - is I wondered whether we ought to be having this discussion with the witness still present in the room in light of some of the matters that Mr. Praljak was actually touching on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bench has reached a consensus. We do not object to the fact that technical questions be put related to communications, but we don't wish the -- we would like the cross-examination to focus on what has been addressed during the examination-in-chief. If there is time left, Mr. Praljak will have the floor, but only if there is time left. What we are interested in are the way in which the Defence counsel respond to what the Prosecution has just said. Mr. Kovacic, at this stage you have no question to put as part of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't have any other questions for cross-examination. And to inform you, we initially wanted Mr. Praljak to put his questions in the end because that was natural. We simply didn't have time to arrange this in advance with other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but for me this is very important, and I have to intervene. Since General Praljak is more knowledgeable about this matter than I am, and I have prepared some telecommunications questions for our defence, I wouldn't want to give our reasons now in the presence of the witness, but I think it would be better for Mr. Praljak to start first with his questions. I can inform you in more detail about my reasons if the witness leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If I understood well, you actually do not have any questions covered in examination-in-chief when it comes to the defence of Mr. Prlic. You only have technical questions, and you think that it is only Mr. Praljak who is competent enough to put questions in that area. In that case, we will turn to the next Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I propose that we resume our regular order for cross-examination. We will all bear in mind that Mr. Praljak needs some time for his questions. I also have some technical issues, and I will leave enough time for Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So what is the order to be?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone. My name is Vesna Alaburic, I am attorney-at-law from Zagreb, representing General Milivoj Petkovic here. Mr. Saric, I will be putting some questions to you which are, to my mind, very brief and simple, hoping that this would help us clarify some contradictions and some things that were not clear in your evidence-in-chief. I'm speaking deliberately slowly for the sake of interpretation so that the people who do not speak our language can fully follow. We received from the Prosecutor your statement, given by you on the 29th of August, 2002. That's what it says on the document that we received. My question to you is: Did you really speak to the Prosecution of this Tribunal, and did you really provide this statement on this date?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: In my testimony so far today, that's precisely what I mentioned. I said that sitting at this table here, I wrote a report as to what had been happening to me that day before I was brought there, and that's exactly the statement that you received. It was just retyped. I never saw that statement before. I can't tell you what was written there and then retyped.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, the statement that you're mentioning now is the statement you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? I provided?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You or somebody else. Was it provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Office of the Prosecutor has it, and I saw that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, unfortunately, we do not have the statement that you are referring to. What we received from the OTP is just one statement that you gave to the OTP on the 29th of August, 2002, and it seems unlikely that this is the same statement that you wrote back then while sitting at that table. This is the statement that begins with the following text: "I am here of my own free will to give a statement to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor," and so on. Thus I'm asking you whether on the said day, the 29th of August, 2002, you really gave or signed the statement given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 29th of August, 2002.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Tell us, did you speak to the OTP on the 16th of January, 1998?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will put some questions to you about your statement from 2002 because it is partially contradictory. It contradicts partially what you were saying to us today. Today, you told us that you were arrested by two soldiers. In your 2002 statement, however, you say that there were three soldiers. No. I apologise. In your 1998 statement, you speak of three soldiers. Can you please clarify: Were you arrested by two or three armed persons?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Two. The third one was the driver. I don't know whether he can be considered a soldier. If so, then there were three of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your 1998 statement, you said that you were arrested by the members of the military police of the HVO, whereas today you only mentioned armed soldiers. Therefore, I'm asking you: Were you arrested by the military police members?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was arrested by Franjo Cvitkovic. It should probably be easy to establish where he served at the time. I may be inaccurate because I'm not privy to the records. In my eyes he was a member of the military police or police, but during the war that is always the military police. Now, as to his exact affiliation, you would need to look that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you told us -- you said that you were arrested in the house where you were hiding, and in your 1998 statement you said that you were arrested in your apartment. Can you clarify. Which is true; what you stated in 1998 or what you said today?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was arrested in Ilici in the house which wasn't mine. It wasn't in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give us the name of the owner of the house in which you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: His name was Andjelko. Unfortunately, he's deceased. He died several years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember his last name?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not giving us the last name because you can't remember or because you don't wish for some reason to give us his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no reasons not to give you the last name. If you were to offer me ten last names I would probably pick the right one out of them, but right now it escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saric. I will now be putting questions to you about the Vranica building. Today, you talked to us about the attacks and then you said, "That the building was destroyed in the HVO attacks." It was recorded today on page 15, line 1, of the transcript. Do you know that the Serb forces, in the course of 1992 and 1993, attacked and shelled Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the target of Serb forces, among others, was the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the building was severely damaged by Serb shells?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us to what extent the Serb shells damaged the building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that the position of the building is such that Serb shells could not hit the building. The building was destroyed, damaged from the other side that the Serb shells were not able to reach.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct, then, to conclude that the Serb shells could hit the building only laterally?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The building had damage in many spots, but on that particular day that entire portion of the building where the corps was and the brigade was completely burned down. It was the incendiary shells that hit it, and that part of the building was completely destroyed. It was not usable following that. That's why I said that it was destroyed. It wasn't wrecked and knocked down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was it visible on the photographs of the Vranica building shown to you today by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think so, but don't hold me to it, because these photographs are more of informative nature. The angle is not quite right and there are many obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we please put the photographs to the witness, Exhibit P 09413, page 4. I don't think this is page 4.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: This one. Look at the upper one, in the right corner. You can see that this is damage inflicted by fire. Can you please scroll down. The see this right angle. You see this damage inflicted by fire, by burning. But it wasn't only there. It was in a wider area, both at that height and lower.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, based on this photograph, one could conclude that in the apartments in proximity to that area almost on all floors there were still residents living. You can see that the windows are open, there are flowers on balconies. Do you know whether people continued living in the apartments which were not damaged?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Certainly. There wasn't a building in Mostar which was not in use if it was possible. Only those apartments that were destroyed were abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it then accurate to conclude that the Vranica building wasn't destroyed after all, which is what you stated on page 15 of today's transcript?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. If under "destroyed" you mean razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You just mean that it wasn't usable.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were apartments there were not liveable. If you destroy my chair, then other people may continue sitting in their chairs, but my chair is destroyed. The apartments that burned down were destroyed, and to this day they're not inhabitable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. So you were speaking of individual apartments.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, because this is a huge building, and I said that. I said that it was very long and tall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please slow down, because the interpreters have to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, please tell us, based on your information, the communications system in every army is an important prerequisite for good functioning of the army.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In case of a conflict between two armies, would you say that both of them are trying to learn as much as possible about the communications system of the other one?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Naturally. That's an essential task.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on the rules of warfare, is it standard procedure that one army would try to disable the communications system of the other army?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Depends on the escalation of the conflict and military tactics. I really can't give you an answer to this question. It's not a rule. The rule is that we're trying to learn what the other side has, not that we're trying to destroy it necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you had an alternative whether you wanted to improve or destroy the communications system of the opposing side, what would be your answer?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Under no circumstances would we want to improve the system of the hostile side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time when the 4th Corps of the BH army decided to station its headquarters in the Vranica building, which is a mixed residential and commercial use building and where civilians lived on upper floors, was the BH army command aware that should there be an attack on the BH army, which would necessarily include both the attack on the command and communications system, the civilians would be placed at great risk? Do you know why the BH army command and communications systems were placed in that building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I will answer that with a question. The HVO units were located in many buildings where civilians lived. Take, for example, my street. Many HVO units were stationed in basements in the buildings there. So this is a tactical issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. One day when you have occasion -- thank you, and I apologise. Mr. Saric, this is the command of the BH army that we're talking about. Is it impossible for you to draw a parallel with the HVO command located in the basement of a commercial/residential building? This is why I asked you whether you were aware of the grave risk that you posed to civilians when you headquartered your command in such a building.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Listen, as I have told you, there were 20 to 30 soldiers stationed in that building. It comes nowhere near close to the full strength of the 4th Corps and the brigade. These were just segments of these units. All operative units were stationed outside. This was only a symbolic presence, because if something really important is stationed in a building, then there are more people guarding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an essential question that we wish to pose, and Judge Trechsel will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, who took the decision to locate the centre for communications in the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was most likely a result of a political agreement because they didn't do it on their own. The 4th Corps didn't do it on its own. There was an agreement with the HVO, because there was a cooperation between them and joint action against the Serb enemy, and it was as a result of that that they distributed among themselves locations. Everything was done in agreement. Now, as to which particular people entered into agreement, I wouldn't be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You gave us some important elements, but this decision to locate the communications system in the basement, everybody knows that every army in this world values highly its communications system. Knowing that there was civilians living there, in the basement, do you believe that the decision to place the communications system in the basement was a reasonable one, because in the event of a conflict with Serbs or anybody else, it was evident that shells would be landing on the building where civilians resided? That was the question put to you, and I wanted to reiterate that. What do you as chief of communications system think of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, listen: There are communications systems built and none of the buildings were built purposely for placing the communications centre there. There were some barracks and there were some parts inside those barracks that were used for the armies of both HVO and BH army. BH army was in the southern part, and in the Tihomir Misic barracks was the HVO. Therefore, it was normal for them to select spots in town where certain units would be stationed. That was the deployment. But what the 4th Corps had and what its communications centre was was just a segment in the communications system of the BH army. It was just a part of it, and it simply lost significance overnight, but the whole system continued functioning from other locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, you told us that the HVO was stationed in the Tihomir Misic barracks in the so-called North Camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of attempts of the HVO to agree with the 4th Corps of the BH army about the relocation to the South Camp or, rather, about the relocation of the 4th Corps command from the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about these attempts; how they arose, who negotiated?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know about these details. It wasn't within my purview. I know, however, that the initial intention was to relocate. It was up to the command to decide which unit is important. Perhaps it's important for you but not for the command. The army was headquartered in the Mostar hotel, which we saw in one of the photographs. The agreement was reached there to demilitarise that building. That is to say to have the army leave the building so that there would be nobody else there. And do you know what happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: As soon as the BH army left that building, the HVO soldiers entered it and they never left. That was the agreement which wasn't observed. Who failed to observe it, why, whether such an agreement existed, I don't know that, but that's what I can tell you. Therefore, everything else was possible. Whatever comes to mind was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It's 12.30. We have to take a break. We shall continue in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have one hour left, so you need to finish in the time we have left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have only two more questions. I think I will need only three or four minutes. Could we please have in e-court Defence document of General Praljak number 3D 00016. And because I didn't know we would need the document, I did not prepare it in the file for Your Honours and for my learned friends, but I do hope that it will be enough to remind ourselves of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, I assume you can see that this is a document which on the 21st of April, 1993, was signed by Mr. Arif Pasalic and Petar Zelenika. Could you please read for us item 1 of this communique.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: "A common or Joint Command will be issued for the removal of all soldiers of the army of BH --" The letter R is missing, the army of the Republic of BH -- "to Konjic, Juzni Logor, and the HVO to the Tihomir Misic barracks and the Heliodrom barracks. The 3rd Brigade remains in the existing building or facility and moves only toward the enemy line. The deadline is 48 hours after the issuing of this order. The 23rd of April at 1300 hours."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, can you tell us whether the HVO complied with this agreement? To the best of your knowledge. If I can remind you, you've already told us that the HVO was in Tihomir Misic barracks.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Tihomir Misic, but we haven't finished what we were saying before about the Mostar hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But our topic is the Vranica building, not the Mostar hotel. We don't have time to go into it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I haven't said everything I have to say about that building. There's something I wanted to say about it. The Vranica building, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask you anything about that hotel, so please let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Sorry, about the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, to the best of your knowledge, did the army of BH comply with this agreement of the 21st of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I think it did. This is the deployment such as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the army of BH leave the Vranica building and deploy all its members in the locations mentioned in this communique; in Konak and in Juzni Logor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: What do you mean; all soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was the Vranica building abandoned or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions about this topic. My last question I will skip over a lot of things because of shortage of time. Could we have in e-court document 4D 00071. Mr. Saric, could you please read through this statement very quickly. These -- this is the record of your interview carried out on the 10th of July, 1993, and it was compiled by Mr. Frano Primorac and Toni Ramljak, who are members of the military police administration, the SIS, and can you tell us whether this is your authentic statement. Is this what you really said during your interview?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: There's a lot here that was said, but they wrote this up in the way that suited them. This is not complete. Well, I can't say now because it was a long time ago, but I wrote my statement in handwriting, and this was typed out several days later. I don't know who typed it out. I didn't see any Ramljak or the other person you mentioned, so somebody did this without me. And what is written here is full of silly things that I would never -- or it's been reformulated. There are a lot of facts here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: By your leave, one last question: From what you say, it follows that the statement that you wrote out in your handwriting in that room at that small desk differs from this record of your interview.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, quite certainly the outline was the same, but I don't believe that the phrases are mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, no, because this is written in the Croatian language and you speak differently. But the phrases are not important, it's the essence, the meaning.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, there are many things here that are not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that your handwritten statement is materially different from this record?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No, not materially.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, due to shortage of time, I will not put any more questions. Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you, Mr. Saric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is Defence counsel asked -- going to ask to have this document tendered into evidence, number 71?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document of General Praljak's defence, D3 0016 has already been admitted, and we tender document 4D 00071.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Chamber will rule on the matter. When looking at the statement in B/C/S -- at the document in B/C/S, there is no signature under the name. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to be as brief as possible, but I wish to leave some time should Mr. Coric, the accused, decide to ask a few questions. Cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saric, I'm Dijana Tomasegovic Tomic, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Valentin Coric in these proceedings. I would like to start right away, and I wish to clarify a few points in your testimony which I don't understand clearly. If I understood you correctly, you spent the time from the 7th to the 9th of July at the faculty of mechanical engineering. The 10th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was overlapping between the question and the answer. The interpreter did not hear the answer. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm confused about this.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: You'll remain confused. It was a long time ago. I can't recall all the details. It's as it's written down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, then, we'll go day by day just to clarify, and perhaps this can jog your memory: You were arrested on the 7th of July and brought to the faculty of mechanical engineering. There you spent the night. You were brought to a room where you wrote a statement on the first day, then you spent the night, as far as I could understand. What happened on the following day, the 8th of July?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Just waiting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just waiting. And then we come to the third day, the 9th of July. There's another night. And then on the third day you were interviewed. That's the 9th of July, according to my calculation. And was that the day on which you left the faculty?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. If I understood you correctly, you said that you did not leave the room where you were put except for when you were taken for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Only -- I didn't leave the basement. I did leave the room. I could go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So could we clarify. In your statement you said that for a full three days you did not use the toilet because you had no need because you were given nothing to eat or drink.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: So I didn't walk about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't walk about, you remained in your room. Could I get a yes or no answer. Does that mean that you were in your room, that you weren't walking about? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Does that mean whether I used the toilet or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you leave your room for any other reason except for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I went to the toilet once, but when I saw that dead man there, I came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what day that was when you saw that man?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That happened in the course of those three days. The last day. I think it was the last day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I understand that you want to gain time, but you do not gain time by speaking fast and overlapping all the time, because that makes us interrupt you and tell you that you have to slow down. The poor interpreter is completely breathless and we want to be sure that we hear everything Counsel and the witness say. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I'll be careful.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said, then, that you went out only on that third day, the 9th, to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: To the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in your statement you said there were two rooms, one of which you call the torture chamber and the other one you call the slaughterhouse.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During those three days while you were in that basement, did you personally see any torture or any execution in the rooms referred to as the torture chamber or the slaughterhouse?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: The first night we spent there a group of soldiers arrived, and they used flashlights, looking for someone. In the night I couldn't see anyone, but they were hitting someone in that group, and from the room where the people from Konjic were we heard that they were beating someone. Whether they were beating that man who died or someone else, I don't know, but that night there was a beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So two rooms away from your room, not in the room called the torture chamber.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you can imagine this. This was an open space. The cells 1, 2, 3, the torture chamber, this was all basically the same space, it was all so close. If you were standing at the door it was like being in the other room. It was all one area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you can't say precisely where this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It was taking place in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the basement, but you can't pinpoint the exact spot.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not important.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you or can't you say? Don't tell me whether it's important. Just tell me whether you can or you can't.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking whether you know precisely where what you heard was taking place. You say you heard a beating. Can you pinpoint the precise location where this was happening or can you only say that it was in the basement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It was in the basement, between cell 3 and the torture chamber. Whether it was more inside or more outside or at the very edge I can't say, but it was in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I now wish to go back to the part of your statement where you said that you saw a person you referred to as Hebibovic, but you're not sure. You saw dead in the corridor and then you decided not to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My colleague Ms. Alaburic, during her examination, put to you the statement you made to the Prosecutors of this Tribunal on the 16th of January, 1998. Let me remind you now of a part of that statement. In that statement you say: "A man arrived in our room from the next room. He was from the village of Glavaticevo, Konjic municipality. He told me that they had been taken prisoner near a stream or a creek near the Salakovac hydroelectric power plant. He said these were civilians. They were beaten on the first day, and we heard the sounds of a beating. One of them was lying on the floor in the corridor. His name was Hebibovic. I don't know his first name. People from our room who were passing him by and they saw him lying there and heard him screaming." In this statement of yours I cannot find any reference to you yourself seeing this man lying in the corridor. So could you please clarify this discrepancy between what we heard today what I read out to you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Madam, all this was taking place in an area 15 or 20 square metres. Everybody knew everything that was happening. There were some spots from which you couldn't see something because of the angle, but you could use your ears and all your other senses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please, we have very little time. Can you explain whether you saw this man lying on the floor or whether you just heard about it from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I heard about it, and then, when I went to the toilet, I saw him myself. I knew that he was there. He was already dead at the time I passed by him. Up to that time, we heard him moaning less and less frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So today you say that you saw him.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I saw him lying on the floor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your examination today you said that you had already testified before a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a case against -- against several accused one of whom was Zeljko Dzidic. Was this before the county court in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what court it was. Ibro Bulic was the name of the Prosecutor. I don't know whether it's the cantonal or some other court.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you were heard in a court in Mostar in proceedings against Mr. Dzidic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, today you said that you were not heard concerning the circumstances you testified about today during these proceedings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. I apologise. In these proceedings in Mostar, were you also questioned about the situation at the faculty of mechanical engineering?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When I said that it wasn't about this topic, I thought about the Heliodrom and other things, not just the faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court Exhibit 5D 00515. We have the document, but before we start with it, let me ask you this: In those proceedings, did you give evidence about the murder of Hebibovic, the person that you saw lying?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I think that that was the main issue, but I'm not sure. But you should have everything in the court records.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness to glance at the text on this page, except for what was crossed out, and to refresh his memory as to whether this is the evidence he gave in that trial in Mostar. Mr. Saric, would you please let me know when you are done reading these last two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I just finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we see page 2, please. Would you please read -- can it be enlarged? Can you zoom in to the second and third paragraph on this page, please. Second and third paragraph, please. I can read it out to you. That's easier. So in paragraph 2 you say as follows -- the last five lines, it says: "The moaning was heard until the morning. When some people went to the bathroom, they said that they saw a dead man. I didn't go out, and I didn't see him. The man who asked for water from us, I heard from him that the man who was killed was called Hebibovic. He said that he was from the place near Konjic near Glavaticevo." Can you remember whether you stated this before the court in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Most likely. I know, however, that when I went to the toilet I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. Today in your evidence you said that during the three days you spent at the faculty for mechanical engineering you received no water or food; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your evidence today and based on the evidence you gave before, it seems that the person from another room came to your room for water.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: He came to us, asking for water, but there was no water.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. There was no water. Now, please, the same document that we have on our screens now, could we see page 4 of it, please. Page 4. It says page 63 at the top. I will read paragraph 7 to you: "When asked by victim Azra Penava how come there was water in their room and how they received water, the witness stated that he didn't know where the water had come from but that there was a plastic bottle with water, whereas they received the food on the second day." Do you remember saying this in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't know where this came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No, because I don't see the water.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You didn't. Now, let me go to something from the beginning of your evidence which confused me. You said in your statement or, rather, in your evidence, when you were arrested in your friend's house that under the bed on which you slept they found a Kalashnikov but that it wasn't yours but, rather, that of your friend.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Why did your friend put his Kalashnikov under your bed? Did you have some kind of a military role there? Were you a guard there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had another two Kalashnikovs that he kept elsewhere. This was an empty one. Unloaded. There were no -- there was no ammunition there. I didn't know how many more he had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you didn't find it odd that he placed this Kalashnikov under your bed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Odd. No, it wasn't odd.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him about that Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before they found it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't even know that it was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How do you know, then, that it wasn't loaded?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I know it because when they found it they saw that it wasn't loaded, that there was no ammunition there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions. I am now yielding the floor to Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric. ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examination by the Accused Coric:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saric, I'm the accused Coric. Since my Defence counsel exhausted almost all questions, I have just one remaining. What were you doing in hiding from the 9th of May to the 7th of July, 1993? You were in hiding. Were you doing anything else?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I had to kill time. There was a lot of activities. I would read books, repair some electronic equipment, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout that time did you have any contact with your command?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did you reach Ilici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Taking which route?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: From Susinska Buna [phoen] to Rondo, and then from Rondo to Ilici, and then Ilici through the swamps to that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For us who are quite familiar with Mostar, would you say that this is one of the most frequented roads leading to Ilici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the most used.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you call that hiding?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: People from your corps, did they start a search for you when they discovered you were gone?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Upon leaving in April of 1994, were you questioned by the security organs of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Upon leaving the camp, I resumed my duties as chief of communications, and naturally I gave a statement about my experiences in that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since you are quite familiar with the military system, especially wartime responsibilities, what is your comment to this fact that your command knew nothing about you, had no contact with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I had no contact with them, but my wife was alive and she remained in the apartment there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So she was your go-between with the 4th command?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Most likely. And all of my relatives learned that I had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So they knew that you were in Ilici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Not in Ilici, rather, at Heliodrom. Nobody except for my wife knew that I was in Ilici. At least, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I've concluded with this portion. I have just another minor issue. The people that you were with in the so-called confinement cells - and based on what I heard from you those were not really solitary confinement cells because they held up to seven people - how were people designated to go to solitary confinement cells? Because we know that people were also assigned to other floors.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: You should be able to tell us what was the criteria in assigning people to cells.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When we change the roles, then, yes, you can put questions to me. I put this question to you, so you can't respond with a question. I asked you whether you heard of the criteria that was used -- used in order to distribute people to cells.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I supposed, and I said so, that it was done because I was the officer of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were the others all officers with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Mostly. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As I can see, you did have some communication among you staying in different cells. You probably talked to other detainees. Did they tell you who interrogated them, who investigated them before they reached solitary confinement cells?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There was no need for you to talk about them -- to talk to them about this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I've concluded, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have just several questions. I know we are short on time, so I would like to ask Mr. Saric to be as brief as possible so that we leave enough time for other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that upon arriving in Heliodrom you basically didn't know anybody there. I have the HVO structure in mind and the staff.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The only contact you had was with the guards.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the OTP in August of 2002 - I will read a sentence out of it - you say that there was no occasion for you to get acquainted with the command structure at Heliodrom; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Smiljanic. You said that he was the camp commander, responsible for the camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It's correct that I said that I had heard it. Now, as to whether he indeed was in that position, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When asked by His Honour Mindua, you said that you didn't know Mr. Pusic and that you had never seen him and had no contact with him.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Up until today. I don't even know him to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name of Mile Pusic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Pusic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No, none of Pusics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the two statements you gave to the OTP in January of 1998 and August of 2002, you also gave the statement in 1993. It was given to the administration of the military police, and then, immediately upon leaving Heliodrom, you gave a statement to the MUP in Mostar in July of 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And then you gave a statement to the cantonal court in Mostar in 2002. Perhaps you can't remember all of them, but it amounts to five or six statements that you gave about these events where you mentioned many persons who were in a way involved in everything that you had lived through.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I read all of your statements, and I can tell you that in none of them do you mention Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Most likely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At least what I read didn't include his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last Defence counsel before we give the floor to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit I didn't hear you because I didn't have my headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saric, my name is Senka Nozica. I am Defence counsel of Mr. Stojic. I will be putting some very brief questions to you, and I will be true to my word and leave some time for Mr. Praljak. Sir, can you tell me, how did the officials treat you, at least those people that you believed to be officials while you were at the faculty of mechanical engineering?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It was decent in the sense that nobody beat me, if that falls under the category of decent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When speaking of Heliodrom, can you tell me whether, in those locations where you were, there were any Croats.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they stayed there very briefly, and they were mostly either criminals or people who violated military discipline rules. They stayed there very briefly, but there were some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did they stay in the same room with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Just one who stayed there very briefly. He was from Prozor, and I believe his first name was Ante, but he stayed there such a brief period of time that I simply failed to mention him. He was a true criminal, a petty criminal, an informer. He stayed there very briefly and then he left. He was the only person of different ethnicity staying with us. People mentioned a man from Split, and then there were also some drug addicts who had been at the front or I don't know where, and they would tend to stay there a night or two and then they would be released.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please explain, just prior to you being taken to the school of mechanical engineering, what were your duties? You said that you were highly placed officer in the 4th Corps. What were your specific duties? I'm now referring to the period of time just prior to you being taken to the faculty of mechanical engineering. I'm referring to the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I was in charge of communications centre, which ensures communication between the command and subordinate units as well as the commander and his aides, and the command and the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you were a leader of sorts. Did you take part in any negotiations? Did you send any documents signed by you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. No. That was an early stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: No. That was an early stage in the work of the 4th Corps, and that was mostly done by the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you did not send any messages?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I did not send any messages and I didn't sign any orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you personally send any reports or transmit any reports by your hand?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Naturally there was communication and there were reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Written reports.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry for speeding. This is all due to the lack of time. Could we see 2D 00083. Would you please look at this report, and would you please tell us whether this is one of your reports.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting, not my handwriting. Do you still want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is this your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So somebody wrote --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Just my signature. Somebody else wrote it. It's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll read this out to you. A report: "Through the command of the 3rd Corps, strictly confidential, 02-2870-1/93. "We are forwarding the text to keep you informed." The text itself reads as follows: "On the 4th of July, 1993, in the evening hours, in the sector of Scipe --" correct? -- "the HVO was firing from infantry weapons."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I can't follow this because I don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You don't have it on the screen? Is there a problem? Because I have it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I have it on the screen, but I don't see what you're reading now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can that being zoomed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will go on.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: You don't have to go on. I'll tell you what this is about. This is the kind of report that every day the duty officer of the corps sends to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I would like to read it until the end.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Provocations are being carried out with infantry weapons. I sent a patrol which captured and disarmed Ivanko Abram, a member of the 3rd Uzedol Battalion. I then sent a 12-man team to take Vilic hill, the dominant elevation overlooking Ivanici village and Pajici village. From there there is a threat to our forces. During the 8th of April, 1993, the HVO forces wanted to take our forces off Vilic hill with an infantry attack but the attack was beaten back."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, what are you interested in here?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to know whether you remember this report and whether you signed it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember at all, but this -- where it says the content is as follows, this means that this is a report that we received from the ground, and we were forwarding it on. This was the usual kind of thing that happened. Reports would arrive about the situation on the ground and they would be forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. What I want to know is exactly what the situation on the ground was on the 11th of April, 1993. And finally, please, there are a number of contradictions, but I will ask you about another statement that you made which has not been listed where there is also a contradiction between what you say today regarding the alleged death of Mr. Hebibovic. Could we please see in e-court a Prosecution document, ERN number 043775.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: RR 04775.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you recall that during the investigation before the trial at the court in Mostar you made some statements regarding the death of Mr. Hebibovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what do you mean whether I made any statements before my statement in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question was very precise. You made a statement at the trial and my colleague presented part of that statement to you. What I'm asking you is during the investigation stage in this same case, did you give a statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I want to put to you the statement you made during the investigation phase. As far as I can see, this is in English, if this is it. No. In order to save time, I will read out part of that statement to you, and we can put it on the ELMO. This is not ECM. Could you please take it from my colleague and put page 2 on the ELMO. Today, when asked by my colleague Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic about this, you said that it happened on the last day, what happened to Hebibovic, the last day of your stay. Mr. Saric, I asked you a question.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say. In the statement, it's all clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In what statement is it clear? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Well, what we say today.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Today you said --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Before I left, what I learned was that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Today you said, when asked by my colleague, that what happened to Mr. Hebibovic happened on the last day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Of my stay there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at what it says in your statement here, which you gave under oath to the investigating judge in Mostar. That's page 2, and I will read out to you what you said. It's not very legible, but that's what it says here, and this is the part that's underlined: "I don't know -- I do not know any of the accused.
